key_concept: A circular arc carrying current $I$ and subtending angle $\theta$ at the centre gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 I \theta}{4\pi r}$; current splits between parallel paths in inverse ratio of their resistances.
steps: The two semicircles ABC and ADC are in parallel between A and C. With $R_{ABC} = \frac{1}{2}R_{ADC}$, current divides inversely to resistance: $I_{ABC} = \frac{2I_0}{3}$ and $I_{ADC} = \frac{I_0}{3}$.
Each semicircle subtends $\theta = \pi$ at O, so it gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$.
Current flows from A to C in both arcs. Along ABC (left side) the sense is anticlockwise and along ADC (right side) it is clockwise, so the two fields at O are opposite.
The straight lead wires lie along the line through O (the extension of AC), so $d\vec{l} \times \hat{r} = 0$ and they contribute no field at O.
why_not_others: Option (2) $\frac{\mu_0 I_0}{4r}$ comes from adding the two semicircle fields instead of subtracting them, or from using the full current in one arc. Option (3) treats the loop as a full ring carrying $I_0$, and option (4) is the formula for a long straight wire, which does not apply here.
common_trap: Adding the fields of the two arcs, forgetting that currents in parallel arcs circulate in opposite senses about O.
time_saving_tip: Net $B = \frac{\mu_0}{4r}(I_1 - I_2)$ for two parallel semicircles; here $I_1 - I_2 = \frac{I_0}{3}$, giving $\frac{\mu_0 I_0}{12r}$ directly.
